# Database Design Decisions

Concepts (primary keys, indexes, transactions…) are taught in [05_DATABASE](../05_DATABASE/DATABASE_FUNDAMENTALS.md). This page records _why_ the schema looks the way it does.

---

## DB1. UUIDv7 primary keys generated by Postgres (D26, D38)

- **Problem:** every row needs an id that is unique, safe to expose in URLs, and fast to index.
- **Chosen:** `uuid primary key default uuidv7()`.
- **How UUIDv7 works:** 128 bits. The first 48 bits are the Unix time in milliseconds, then a version marker and random bits. Two ids created later sort after earlier ones.
- **Why:**
  - Sequential integers (`1, 2, 3`) leak business numbers ("they have 1,042 users") and let people step through `/users/1042`, `/users/1043`.
  - Random UUIDv4s are safe but land at random places in the B-tree index, so every insert touches a different page; that's slow and fragments the index.
  - UUIDv7 is not guessable in practice, and new ids always go at the "right end" of the index, like integers.
  - Because ids sort by time, "newest first" is `order by id desc`, with no separate `created_at` index needed for paging.
- **Disadvantages:** 16 bytes instead of 8 for a `bigint`. The id reveals its creation time (acceptable: posts show their date anyway).
- **Alternatives:** `bigserial`; UUIDv4; ULID; Snowflake ids.
- **Still appropriate?** Yes. Postgres 18's built-in `uuidv7()` made it free; the seed script even generates UUIDv7s for backdated timestamps so the "Newest" sort matches the displayed dates (D54).

---

## DB2. Two roles: migrator and app (D19, D52, D57, D62)

- **Problem:** if the API is compromised (say, by SQL injection), how much damage can it do?
- **Chosen:** `perspective_app` can only `SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE` rows; `perspective_migrator` owns the schema. `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES` gives the app access to every future table automatically. `audit_log` additionally has `UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE` revoked from the app.
- **What could go wrong without it:** with one all-powerful user, an injection could `DROP TABLE users`, `ALTER` columns, or erase the audit trail.
- **Cost:** two connection strings; the migrator URL must be kept out of the running server (done with `env -u` in the Dockerfile).
- **Still appropriate?** Yes. It's cheap, and it was much cheaper to do on day one than to re-own tables later.

---

## DB3. Case-insensitive uniqueness through expression indexes (D28)

- **Problem:** `Sam@Mail.com` and `sam@mail.com` must be one account; `Sam` and `sam` look like the same person.
- **Chosen:** `unique index on lower(email)` and `on lower(username)`; queries use `where lower(email) = $1`. The original capitalisation is still stored and displayed.
- **Why in the database:** two simultaneous sign-ups could both pass an application check; only a unique index is race-proof.
- **Alternatives:** the `citext` extension (case-insensitive text type); always storing lower-case.
- **Trade-off:** queries must remember `lower(...)` to use the index. `citext` avoids that but is an extension.

---

## DB4. Enums for closed sets of values

- **Chosen:** Postgres enum types: `stance`, `user_role`, `question_status`, `report_reason`, etc. `stance` and `user_role` are built from the **same TypeScript arrays** (`STANCES`, `USER_ROLES`) the frontend uses.
- **Why:** the database rejects any other value; one list of names everywhere.
- **Disadvantages:** adding a value needs a migration (`ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE`); removing one is hard.
- **Alternatives:** `text` + `check (x in (...))`; a lookup table.

---

## DB5. Composite primary keys for "one per person"

- `user_stances (user_id, question_id)`: one stance per person per question (D5).
- `post_votes (user_id, post_id)`: one vote per person per post. A repeated vote becomes `on conflict do nothing`, which makes voting **idempotent** (repeating it changes nothing).
- `oauth_accounts (provider, provider_user_id)`: one Google account can't be linked twice. Plus a unique `(user_id, provider)`: a user can't have two Google accounts.

---

## DB6. Partial unique index: one _live_ post per side (D41)

`unique (author_id, question_id, stance) where deleted_at is null`.

- Deleting your post frees the slot (you can write a new one).
- A **moderator removal does not** free the slot (`removed_at` isn't in the condition), so you can't post a second copy after being moderated (D50).
- Posts stay in the column of the author's stance **at posting time**, even if the author later changes sides (`posts.stance` is a snapshot).

---

## DB7. Stance and vote snapshots (D7, D44)

`post_votes.voter_stance` and `post_votes.weight` are frozen at vote time.

- **Why:** if someone changes their stance, their old votes keep their meaning; scores never need recomputing because of a stance change; unvoting subtracts exactly what was added.
- **Bonus:** because the raw facts (voter stance, post stance) are stored, the weights can be retuned later and every score rebuilt exactly (`pnpm recompute-scores`).

---

## DB8. Adjacency list + recursive CTE for threads (D11, D48)

- **Chosen:** `comments.parent_id` points at the parent comment; `depth` is stored (1–50, checked).
- **Alternatives:**

| Model             | Idea                                     | Pros                               | Cons                                                              |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Adjacency list ✅ | Each row stores its parent               | Simple inserts; easy to understand | Reading a subtree needs recursion (Postgres does it in one query) |
| Materialised path | Each row stores `/a/b/c`                 | Subtree = prefix match             | Paths must be maintained; long strings                            |
| Nested sets       | Left/right numbers per node              | Fast subtree reads                 | Inserting renumbers many rows (bad for a live discussion)         |
| Closure table     | A table of all ancestor/descendant pairs | Flexible queries                   | Many extra rows per insert                                        |

- **Why stored `depth`:** checking "is this reply too deep?" needs only the parent's depth, not a walk up the tree.

---

## DB9. Generated `tsvector` column + GIN index for search (D39)

`search_vector tsvector generated always as (setweight(to_tsvector('english', title), 'A') || setweight(to_tsvector('english', description), 'B'))`.

- Postgres keeps it current automatically on every insert or update: no triggers, no application code.
- Title words weigh more (A) than description words (B) in `ts_rank`.
- English stemming: "voting", "votes" and "voted" all match "vote".
- **Alternative:** a search engine (Meilisearch, Elasticsearch). Measured and rejected for now (D72).

---

## DB10. Trigram index for "did you mean…?" (D39)

`gin (title gin_trgm_ops)` + `title % $1` (similarity above a threshold), ordered by `similarity()`. Trigrams are three-letter chunks, so typos and partial titles still match, which full-text search can't do.

---

## DB11. Stored counters with transactional maintenance (Phase 4, D74)

See [A7 in ARCHITECTURAL_DECISIONS](ARCHITECTURAL_DECISIONS.md#a7-store-derived-counters-updated-in-the-same-transaction-phase-4-d74). Migration `0011` added the question counters **and backfilled** them from existing stances in the same migration, so the deployed data was correct the moment the code started using it.

---

## DB12. Polymorphic references for reports and the audit log (D50)

`reports (target_type, target_id)` can point at a question, post, challenge or comment.

- **Why:** one review queue for four kinds of content.
- **Cost:** no foreign key is possible, so the database can't guarantee the target exists. The code handles a missing target: the queue shows "This content no longer exists" (`preview: null`).
- **Alternatives:** four nullable FK columns with a check that exactly one is set; four report tables.

---

## DB13. Indexes match queries exactly (D66, D74)

Two lessons measured in Phase 9 and after:

1. A **partial index's `WHERE`** must match the query's filter. With `where deleted_at is null` only, Postgres couldn't use the index for a query that also filters `removed_at is null` _in order_, so it read the whole column and sorted it (3.0 ms, 1,729 pages). Matching the condition: 0.4 ms, 95 pages.
2. **Sort direction and NULLS order** must match. `order by x desc` means `NULLS FIRST` in Postgres. The first index was built `DESC NULLS LAST` (Drizzle's default output), so Postgres had to add an incremental sort step. Migration `0012` rebuilt it `NULLS FIRST`: 3.4 ms → 0.5 ms.

Details: [INDEXING_AND_QUERY_OPTIMIZATION.md](../05_DATABASE/INDEXING_AND_QUERY_OPTIMIZATION.md).

---

## DB14. Timestamps with time zone, everywhere

`timestamp with time zone` (`timestamptz`) stores an absolute instant. A server in Singapore, a developer laptop in another time zone and CI in the US all agree on what "now" means. Plain `timestamp` stores wall-clock time without a zone and is ambiguous.
